lead: This unit turns coordinates into pictures: move and resize shapes with matrices, decide which rectangle of the world the screen shows, throw away what falls outside it, and project a 3D scene through a camera. After it you can transform any polygon by hand, map it to a viewport, and clip a line or a polygon to a window without guessing.
about: Unit 2 is about moving geometry and then deciding how much of it reaches the screen. 2.1 gives the five 2D transforms as coordinate formulas. 2.2 rewrites them as 3×3 matrices using homogeneous coordinates, 2.3 multiplies those matrices into one composite, and 2.4 lifts the same idea to 4×4 matrices in 3D. 2.5 maps a chosen window of the world onto a viewport on the display. 2.6 and 2.7 clip lines and polygons to that window, so nothing outside is ever drawn. 2.8 puts the scene behind a camera and projects it to 2D, parallel or perspective. Together the chapters take a shape from its own coordinates to its final pixels.

chapters.idea: Every 2D transform is a rule that moves each point (x, y) to a new point (x′, y′).
chapters.depth: Translation by (tx, ty), rotation by θ about the origin and about a pivot point, scaling by (sx, sy) about the origin and about a fixed point, and shear in x and y. Give the coordinate formulas first, then the 2×2 matrix each one produces. Some syllabi also list reflection and call the whole family affine transformations; show reflection about the x axis, the y axis and the line y = x in one short block. Fix the sign convention: in maths, positive θ is counter-clockwise with y pointing up; on a display with y pointing down the same θ looks clockwise, so say which convention you are using. Stop before matrices are combined.

figure.title: One point through three transforms
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain in which a point is scaled, then rotated, then translated, giving the final point.

chapters.example: Rotate the triangle A(0,0), B(2,0), C(0,2) by θ = 90° counter-clockwise about the origin. With cos 90° = 0 and sin 90° = 1 the rule is x′ = x·cos θ − y·sin θ = −y and y′ = x·sin θ + y·cos θ = x. So A → A′(0,0), B → B′(0,2), C → C′(−2,0). Side lengths 2, 2 and 2√2 are unchanged and the right angle at A stays a right angle, which is the check that rotation is rigid.
chapters.trap: Rotating about the origin when the question says about a point such as (2, 1), and forgetting that screen coordinates grow downwards, so a positive θ looks clockwise on a display.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: points, pixels and the raster grid.
chapters.leave: Homogeneous form and matrix combination to 2.2 and 2.3; drawing the transformed edges to the line algorithms in Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Adding a third coordinate of 1 turns translation into a matrix multiply, so every 2D transform becomes one 3×3 matrix.
chapters.depth: Homogeneous coordinates (x, y, W) with W = 1 for a position and W = 0 for a direction; how to convert back by dividing by W. The 3×3 layout with tx, ty in the last column and the fixed last row 0 0 1. Show why a 2×2 matrix cannot express translation, which is the whole reason for the extra coordinate. Write translation, rotation and scaling as explicit 3×3 matrices and multiply them by hand. Some syllabi call this the homogeneous representation or the homogeneous transformation matrix. Mention that 3D uses a 4×4 matrix with a 1 in the fourth slot.

figure.title: Point and 3×3 matrix in homogeneous form
figure.aria: Four rows of three cells: the homogeneous point (x, y, 1) and the three rows of the matrix, with the translation column marked.

chapters.example: Write translation by tx = 5, ty = 3 as the matrix with rows [1, 0, 5], [0, 1, 3], [0, 0, 1] and apply it to P(2, 1). x′ = 1×2 + 0×1 + 5 = 7 and y′ = 0×2 + 1×1 + 3 = 4, with W′ = 1, so P′ = (7, 4). The same point written as a 2×2 product would need an extra addition step, which the matrix now removes.
chapters.trap: Putting tx and ty in the third row instead of the third column, and translating a direction vector that has W = 0.
chapters.prereq: 2.1: the coordinate formulas for the individual transforms.
chapters.leave: Multiplying matrices into one composite to 2.3; the 4×4 version to 2.4.

chapters.idea: Multiplying the matrices in the order the transforms are applied gives one matrix that does the whole job.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Composition rule M = Mn · … · M2 · M1 for transforms applied M1 first, and the fact that order matters: rotation and translation do not commute. Fixed-point rotation as T(px, py) · R(θ) · T(−px, −py) and scaling about a fixed point the same way. Work one 2×2 and one 3×3 product by hand. Note the practical gain: with many vertices, build M once and apply it to each vertex. Mention that the same rule gives reflection about an arbitrary line as a product of three matrices.

figure.title: Rotation about a fixed point as three matrices
figure.aria: Three matrices in a row — shift the pivot to the origin, rotate, shift it back — combining into the single matrix M.

chapters.example: Rotate (3, 1) by 90° counter-clockwise about the fixed point (1, 1). Shift: (3 − 1, 1 − 1) = (2, 0). Rotate 90°: (x, y) → (−y, x) gives (0, 2). Shift back: (0 + 1, 2 + 1) = (1, 3). The single matrix is M = T(1, 1) · R(90°) · T(−1, −1); its top two rows are [0, −1, 2] and [1, 0, 0], and M × (3, 1, 1) gives (1, 3, 1).
chapters.trap: Writing M = R · T when the translation happens first; the rightmost matrix acts on the point first, so the product reads right to left.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 for the individual transforms and 2.2 for the 3×3 form.
chapters.leave: Numerical shortcuts and the 3D composite case to 2.4; curve deformation to the spline chapter in Unit 3.

chapters.idea: The same transforms act on (x, y, z) with one extra axis, and each one is a 4×4 matrix.
chapters.depth: 3D translation; rotation about the x, y and z axes with the standard sign convention; rotation about an arbitrary axis, stated as a formula and applied once, not derived. Scaling about the origin and about a fixed point, and 3D reflection in a coordinate plane. Say clearly that 3D is right-handed in most textbooks while screen depth can be left-handed. Some syllabi call this three-dimensional geometric and modelling transformations. Show one composite: scale, then rotate, then translate.

figure.title: A 4×4 homogeneous matrix in 3D
figure.aria: A 4×4 grid of cells for the 3D matrix, with the three translation entries and the final 1 marked.

chapters.example: Rotate P(1, 0, 0) by 90° about the z axis, then translate by (0, 0, 5). The z rotation uses x′ = x·cos θ − y·sin θ = 0 and y′ = x·sin θ + y·cos θ = 1, so the point becomes (0, 1, 0). Translation changes only the z entry, giving (0, 1, 5). Rotation about z leaves z = 0 untouched, which confirms the axis convention.
chapters.trap: Mixing up the x, y and z rotation matrices, and using the wrong sign for rotation about y, where the right-hand rule flips the sine terms.
chapters.prereq: 2.2 and 2.3: homogeneous form and matrix products.
chapters.leave: Polygon meshes, quadrics and spline surfaces to Unit 3; the camera and projection stage to 2.8.

chapters.idea: The window-to-viewport map is a scale plus a shift that puts a chosen part of the world onto a chosen part of the screen.
chapters.depth: Define world coordinates, window (the rectangle of the world we want) and viewport (the rectangle on the display where it goes). Derive sx = (xvmax − xvmin) / (xwmax − xwmin) and sy = (yvmax − yvmin) / (ywmax − ywmin), then the mapping formulas xv = xvmin + (xw − xwmin)·sx and yv = yvmin + (yw − ywmin)·sy. Show the same map as a 3×3 matrix. Discuss keeping the aspect ratio equal so circles stay circles; if sx ≠ sy the picture stretches. Name normalization and device coordinates in one line. Some syllabi call this the 2D viewing transformation.

figure.title: 2D viewing pipeline
figure.aria: A left-to-right chain from world coordinates through the chosen window, an optional normalizing stage and the viewport, ending in device coordinates.

chapters.example: Window from (0, 0) to (10, 5) and viewport from (0, 0) to (200, 100). Then sx = (200 − 0)/(10 − 0) = 20 and sy = (100 − 0)/(5 − 0) = 20, so the aspect ratio is preserved. The window point (5, 2.5) maps to xv = 0 + (5 − 0)×20 = 100 and yv = 0 + (2.5 − 0)×20 = 50, that is (100, 50), the centre of the viewport.
chapters.trap: Swapping the words window and viewport, and dividing by the window size while forgetting to subtract the window minimum, which shifts the whole picture.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 and 2.2: transforms and their matrix form.
chapters.leave: What happens to the parts that fall outside the window to 2.6; the 3D version of the pipeline to 2.8.

chapters.idea: Clipping a line means keeping the part inside the window and computing the exact crossing points.
chapters.depth: Cohen–Sutherland: the four region-code bits (top, bottom, right, left), code 0000 for inside, trivial accept when both codes are zero, trivial reject when the bitwise AND is not zero, otherwise intersect with one boundary and repeat. Give the intersection formulas for a vertical boundary x = xmin and a horizontal one y = ymin. Liang–Barsky: parametric form, p and q values, and the u1 = max(0, r), u2 = min(1, r) update rule. Trace each algorithm by hand. Mention Nicholl–Lee–Nicholl by name only. Depth: code outline plus hand tracing, no optimisation proofs.

figure.title: Cohen–Sutherland decision loop
figure.aria: A flowchart that computes end-point codes, accepts or rejects the line, and otherwise intersects with a boundary and loops back with the new endpoint.

chapters.example: Clip the line from P1(−2, 1) to P2(10, 7) against the window x from 2 to 8 and y from 2 to 6. P1 has code 0001 (left of the window); P2 has code 0000, so the AND is zero and the line is not rejected. Parametric form: x = −2 + 12t, y = 1 + 6t with t from 0 to 1. Setting x = 2 gives t = 1/3, so y = 1 + 2 = 3 and the entry point is (2, 3). Setting x = 8 gives t = 10/12 = 5/6, so y = 1 + 5 = 6 and the exit point is (8, 6), which lies on the top boundary and is still inside. The clipped line runs from (2, 3) to (8, 6).
chapters.trap: Clamping a coordinate to the boundary while leaving the other coordinate unchanged, which slides the endpoint off the line; the intersection must be computed along the line.
chapters.prereq: 2.5: window and viewport geometry; Unit 1: line drawing with DDA and Bresenham.
chapters.leave: Circle and ellipse clipping and 3D view volumes to later reading; polygon clipping to 2.7.

chapters.idea: Clip a polygon by clipping its list of edges against one window boundary at a time.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Sutherland–Hodgman: four passes, left, right, bottom, top, and the four cases for each edge — both ends inside output the second vertex, inside to outside output the intersection, outside to inside output the intersection then the second vertex, both outside output nothing. Stress that the output list of one pass is the input of the next, and that the edge from the last vertex back to the first must be included. Name Weiler–Atherton for concave polygons and holes. Mention the degenerate zero-length edge that clipping can leave.

figure.title: Sutherland–Hodgman passes
figure.aria: Four clipping passes in a downward chain, each feeding its output vertex list to the next boundary, ending in the final polygon.

chapters.example: Clip the square with vertices (0, 0), (4, 0), (4, 4), (0, 4) against the window x from 1 to 3 and y from 1 to 3. Left pass at x = 1: the edge (0, 4) → (0, 0) is outside, the edge (0, 0) → (4, 0) crosses at (1, 0) and enters, and the edge (4, 4) → (0, 4) crosses at (1, 4) and leaves. Right pass at x = 3 cuts those at (3, 0) and (3, 4). Bottom pass at y = 1 turns (1, 0) and (3, 0) into (1, 1) and (3, 1). Top pass at y = 3 turns (1, 4) and (3, 4) into (1, 3) and (3, 3). The output is the square (1, 1), (3, 1), (3, 3), (1, 3).
chapters.trap: Doing all four boundaries in one pass over the original vertices, or dropping the closing edge, which loses a corner of the result.
chapters.prereq: 2.6: line clipping and the window boundaries.
chapters.leave: Hidden surface removal and BSP trees to Unit 3; filling the clipped polygon to the scan-fill chapter in Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A 3D scene becomes a 2D picture when a camera defines the view and a projection flattens it.
chapters.depth: Viewing coordinates from three camera parameters: eye position, look-at point and up vector; the view matrix as a rotation plus a translation, stated, not derived. Parallel (orthographic) projection versus perspective. The perspective divide x′ = x·d/z, y′ = y·d/z for a projection plane at z = d with the centre of projection at the origin. Vanishing points and one-, two- and three-point perspective; the view volume, a box for parallel and a frustum for perspective, and why clipping happens in that volume. One line on camera models feeding pose estimation and AR, since some syllabi list those.

figure.aria: A two-level tree splitting projections into parallel, with orthographic and oblique children, and perspective, with one-, two- and three-point children.

chapters.example: Project the point P(2, 4, 6) with the centre of projection at the origin and the projection plane at z = 3. The divide gives x′ = x·d/z = 2×3/6 = 1 and y′ = y·d/z = 4×3/6 = 2, so the screen point is (1, 2). A second point farther away at (2, 4, 12) lands at (0.5, 1), closer to the centre of the picture, which is the size fall-off that makes perspective look real.
chapters.trap: Dividing by z when the plane is at some other depth, and applying a perspective divide in a parallel projection where no divide exists.
chapters.prereq: 2.4 for 3D transforms, 2.5 for window-to-viewport and 2.6 for clipping to the view volume.
chapters.leave: Lighting and shading to Unit 3; camera raw files and photo correction to Unit 5.
